246.title: The direct path
246.hook: a direct path for the purification of beings: four foundations of mindfulness (MN 10)
246.howItsDone: The Satipatthana Sutta is studied and practiced across the Buddhist world, especially in Theravada communities, where many meditation methods, including the Burmese insight traditions, trace themselves to it; the longer version is sometimes chanted in full.

segments.voice: Yesterday: your immeasurables, all four rooms in one sitting. Your line was immeasurable. Day two hundred forty-six, and a new part of the path.

Mindfulness is everywhere now: on apps, in office trainings, on the side of a tea box. Some of it traces back, one way or another, to an old text: a talk the Buddha is said to have given to the people of Kuru, in a market town called Kammasadhamma. For the next three weeks, you'll walk through it, section by section. It's long, and it repeats itself on purpose. Today: the opening line, and the map.
screen: `MINDFULNESS, ON A TEA BOX.` → `ONE OLD TEXT.` → `THREE WEEKS, SECTION BY SECTION.`

segments.voice: The text is the Satipatthana Sutta, number ten in the Middle Length Discourses, with a longer twin, the Maha-satipatthana, in the Long Discourses. Sati means mindfulness, remembering to be present. Patthana is usually taken as foundation or establishing, though scholars argue about how to split the word. So: the establishing of mindfulness. It opens with a bold claim. This, the Buddha says, is the ekayana path, for the purification of beings, for getting past sorrow and lamentation, for the ending of pain and grief, for finding the true way, for realizing nibbana. Ekayana is a puzzle. Some older English translations said the only way. Others say the direct path, or the one-way path, a road that goes straight to one place. The word can bear several meanings, and teachers disagree. Then the map: four foundations, four places to set mindfulness down. The body. Feelings, meaning the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of experience. The mind, its states and moods. And dhammas, a hard word here, often translated mental qualities or phenomena: the patterns the Buddha taught people to recognize. One path, four doors into it. Every section that follows fits somewhere on this map, so when you get lost in the next three weeks, come back to these four.
screen: `SATI + PATTHANA: ESTABLISHING MINDFULNESS.` · `EKAYANA: ONLY, OR DIRECT?` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `ONE PATH, FOUR DOORS.` · then, large: `ONE WAY, FOUR DOORS.`

segments.voice: Touch each door once: body, the weight and contact where you sit; feelings, whether this moment is pleasant, unpleasant or neither; mind, the mood right now, calm, restless, tired. Dhammas: is anything pulling at you, a want, an irritation, a doubt? Name the four quietly, body, feelings, mind, dhammas, and then just sit with the breath.
Satipatthana. The establishing of mindfulness, set down in four places: body, feelings, mind and dhammas.
Your line: one way, four doors. Body, feelings, mind and dhammas, one map. Day two hundred forty-six.

a breathing exercise to calm stress quickly
a vow to meditate every day for life

pairs: the market town of the Kurus

some older translations said so; others say 'the direct path', and teachers disagree.
the sutta has a longer twin in the Long Discourses
the Maha-satipatthana Sutta, DN 22.
'feelings' here means emotions like love or anger
it means the tone of experience: pleasant, painful or neither.

fork.setup: you're lost in a long text with many sections. what does the opening of the Satipatthana Sutta give you?
options: a list of rules.
a map: four foundations every section fits into.

fork.reveal: the opening sets out four foundations, body, feelings, mind and dhammas, and the rest of the sutta fills them in.

what it means: mindfulness set down in four places: body, feelings, mind, dhammas.

247.title: Ardent, aware, mindful
247.hook: the refrain: ardent, clearly knowing, mindful, putting aside longing and dismay (MN 10)
247.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions describe right effort with the image of a well-tuned lute, and the refrain 'ardent, clearly knowing, mindful' is often taught as a checklist for a good sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was satipatthana, the establishing of mindfulness. Your line: one way, four doors. Body, feelings, mind, dhammas.

Heat is an odd thing to ask for in meditation. The usual picture of a meditator is cool: still water, a calm face, nothing burning. Yet when the Satipatthana Sutta describes someone practicing, the first quality it names is a kind of heat. Other texts set a warning right beside it. Too little fire, and you sit and drift. Too much, and you push until something breaks. The sutta repeats one refrain for every foundation, and its first word is about exactly this balance.
screen: `HEAT, IN A TEXT ABOUT CALM?` → `TOO LITTLE, TOO MUCH.` → `THE REFRAIN'S FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: Every time the sutta introduces a foundation, it describes the one practicing with the same four phrases. Ardent. Clearly knowing. Mindful. Having put aside longing and dismay for the world. Ardent, in Pali atapi, comes from tapa, heat: the warmth of real interest, the fire that keeps you coming back. Clearly knowing, sampajano, means understanding what you're doing while you do it. Mindful, satima, is the one who remembers to stay present, who doesn't drift off. The last phrase names what gets set aside: abhijjha and domanassa, wanting and discontent, the grab toward what you like and the sag of dismay at what you don't. So the refrain is a little portrait of a meditator: warm, clear, present, and not pulled around. Why heat? Without it, mindfulness goes limp, and you drift. Another text pairs it with gentleness, in a story about a monk named Sona. Before he was a monk, Sona had been skilled at the lute. He practiced walking meditation so hard his feet bled. The Buddha asked him about his lute. Strings too tight? It wouldn't play. Too loose? It wouldn't play either. Tuned just right, it sang. So ardent never means harsh. It means warm enough to stay, gentle enough to last.
screen: `ARDENT, CLEARLY KNOWING, MINDFUL.` · `ATAPI: FROM TAPA, HEAT.` · `SET ASIDE WANTING AND DISMAY.` · `SONA'S LUTE: NOT TOO TIGHT.` · then, large: `ARDENT AND GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Watch whatever arises, breath, sounds, sensations, with a little warmth, as if this breath were worth noticing. Then check your grip: if your jaw or forehead is tight, let it soften, warm and soft at once. If you drift, come back without scolding; if you're straining, loosen one notch, until the string sings.
Ardent. Atapi, from the word for heat: the warm, steady interest that keeps mindfulness alive, never harsh.
Your line: ardent and gentle. Not too tight, not too loose. That's day two hundred forty-seven.

pushing yourself as hard as you possibly can
a cool, detached calm with no feeling at all

the Buddha's lute story says strings too tight won't play.

trapdoor: what you thought: ardent means intense, pushing hard.

what a scholar hears: ātāpī shares its root with tapas, the ascetic 'heat' of Indian religion; the sutta keeps the warmth but, with Sona's lute, rejects strain.

248.title: The body: breathing
248.hook: gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, breathing in long, he knows it (MN 10)
248.howItsDone: Mindfulness of breathing (anapanasati) is among the most widely taught Buddhist meditations; practitioners sit upright and simply know each breath as long or short, then widen to the whole body and let it calm.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ardent, warm interest that never turns harsh, like Sona's lute tuned just right. Your line was ardent and gentle. Today, the first foundation.

You've breathed about twenty thousand times since yesterday morning. You noticed maybe three: once climbing the stairs, once in a sigh, once when something scared you. The rest happened without you. The breath is your most faithful companion. It never takes a day off, and almost nobody pays it any attention. The Satipatthana Sutta starts its tour of the four foundations right here: with the body, and within the body, the breath.
screen: `TWENTY THOUSAND BREATHS.` → `YOU NOTICED THREE.` → `THE FIRST FOUNDATION.`

segments.voice: The sutta sets the scene simply. A practitioner goes to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, legs crossed, body upright, and sets mindfulness in front of them. Then the instruction. Breathing in long, they know, I breathe in long. Breathing out long, they know, I breathe out long. Breathing in short, they know, I breathe in short. Breathing out short, they know that too. Notice what isn't there: no command to breathe long, no counting, no special technique, no forcing. The breath does what it does, and the practitioner knows it. That's the first step: knowing. Two more follow. They train themselves to breathe in and out experiencing the whole body. And they train themselves to breathe calming the body, letting its activity settle. So the breath is both what you watch and what slowly quiets you. A separate sutta, the Anapanasati Sutta, expands this into sixteen steps; the tradition calls the practice anapanasati, mindfulness of in-and-out breathing. Tradition also says it was the practice the Buddha himself used on the night of his awakening. Why start here? The breath is always available and always now. You can't breathe yesterday's breath. Know this one, and you've arrived in the body, with the other three doors close by.
screen: `THE FOREST, THE TREE, THE EMPTY HUT.` · `BREATHING LONG, THEY KNOW IT.` · `NO FORCING, JUST KNOWING.` · `THE WHOLE BODY, THEN CALMING.` · then, large: `KNOWING THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, as if at the root of a tree, and let the breath come however it comes: if it's long, know it's long; if it's short, know it's short, without adjusting it. After a few breaths, widen to the whole body breathing, belly, chest, shoulders. Then let each out-breath soften something, just a little.
The body, breathing. The first foundation begins with the breath: long, short, the whole body, calming. No forcing, only knowing.
Your line: knowing the breath. Long or short, it's already happening, right now. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 248 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TURNER AT THE LATHE.`

breath control to slow the heart down on purpose

pairs: they know: I breathe in long

options: breathe deeper right away.

fork.reveal: the first step is only knowing. calming comes later, and it comes by itself, not by force.

original.note: Pali ānāpānasati: mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing.

what it means: knowing the breath as it is, long or short, then letting the body calm.

249.title: The turner at the lathe
249.hook: as a skilled turner knows a long pull and a short pull (MN 10)
249.howItsDone: Teachers of mindfulness of breathing often use the sutta's image of the skilled turner to explain that the aim is plain, steady knowing of each breath, like a craftsperson's attention, rather than effortful control.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, breathing. Long, short, the whole body, calming. Your line was knowing the breath. Day two hundred forty-nine.

Watch someone who's really good at a craft. A barber with the clippers. A baker shaping loaves. A carpenter planing a board. They aren't tense, and they aren't daydreaming either. Their hands know exactly what they're doing, stroke by stroke, and it looks almost easy. Right in the middle of the breathing instructions, the Satipatthana Sutta stops to give a picture like that, from a workshop most people have never seen.
screen: `A BARBER, A BAKER, A CARPENTER.` → `HANDS THAT KNOW.` → `A WORKSHOP PICTURE.`

segments.voice: A turner is a woodworker who shapes wood on a lathe, spinning it while a blade carves it round: bowls, legs for a stool, beads. The sutta says: like a skilled turner, or a turner's apprentice. Making a long turn, he knows, I make a long turn. Making a short turn, he knows, I make a short turn. In the same way, the one who meditates, breathing in long, knows I breathe in long; breathing in short, knows I breathe in short. The sutta doesn't describe the machine. It only says the turner knows each pull, long or short, as it happens, all day long. So the picture has a rhythm, like the breath. The image adds three things. First, skill. The turner isn't straining to notice each pull; in skilled hands, the knowing is built in. Mindfulness of breathing is meant to become like that: a skill, not a strain. Second, the turner knows without stopping to comment. No 'what a lovely long pull, I'm so good at this.' Just knowing, and working. Third, the knowing serves the work. A turner who lost track of the pull would ruin the bowl. The breath works the same way. Knowing it isn't an extra task on top of breathing. It's doing breathing well.
screen: `A TURNER SHAPES WOOD ON A LATHE.` · `LONG PULL, SHORT PULL.` · `KNOWING WITHOUT COMMENT.` · `A SKILL, NOT A STRAIN.` · then, large: `THE TURNER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Let each breath be a pull at the turner's lathe, a pull in, a pull out, some long, some short. Just know which is which, the way the turner's hands know, without comment and without changing the breath. If a commentary starts up, let it go, and come back to the next pull.
Skill. Mindfulness of breathing is meant to become this, not a strain: the skilled woodworker knows each long pull and each short pull, and the meditator knows each breath the same way.
Your line: the turner knows. Skilled hands know without narrating. Two hundred forty-nine days in.

a talent you're born with or simply don't have
forcing the breath into a perfect rhythm

250.title: Inside and outside
250.hook: the refrain: in oneself, in others, both; arising and passing away (MN 10)
250.howItsDone: In insight meditation traditions, practitioners return to the sutta's refrain after each exercise: seeing the body, feelings and mind in themselves and in others, and watching them arise and pass away without clinging.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was skill: knowing each pull without comment. Your line was the turner knows. Day two hundred fifty.

Some songs have a chorus that comes back after every verse, and by the end you're singing it without thinking. The Satipatthana Sutta works like that. After every exercise, the breath, the postures, the parts of the body, feelings, the mind, all of it, the same few lines come back. It's easy to skip them as repetition. But some teachers call the chorus the heart of the whole sutta. The verses tell you where to look. The chorus tells you how.
screen: `A CHORUS AFTER EVERY VERSE.` → `EASY TO SKIP.` → `THE VERSES SAY WHERE; THE CHORUS SAYS HOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the chorus, in plain words. The practitioner contemplates the body as a body internally, externally, and both internally and externally. They contemplate its nature of arising, its nature of passing away, and both arising and passing away. Or else mindfulness that there is a body is simply present, just enough for knowing and for continued mindfulness. And they live independent, not clinging to anything in the world. Three pieces. First, inside and outside. Internally means in yourself. Externally is usually explained as in others: the same breath, the same body, the same moods in the person across from you. Commentators and modern teachers read this line a few different ways, and the text doesn't settle it. One reading: what you learn in your own body helps you understand everyone else's. Second, arising and passing away. Whatever you watch, a breath, an itch, a mood, you see it come and go. Watched closely, nothing in it holds still for long. This is the doorway to what Buddhists call impermanence, anicca, not as an idea, but as something you watch happen. Third, independent, not clinging. The knowing is just enough to know. It doesn't grab, doesn't build a story, doesn't need the breath to stay a certain way. Three moves, after every exercise, until they become the way you look at everything.
screen: `THE CHORUS AFTER EVERY EXERCISE.` · `IN ONESELF, IN OTHERS, BOTH.` · `ARISING, PASSING AWAY.` · `JUST ENOUGH TO KNOW, CLINGING TO NOTHING.` · then, large: `IT ARISES, IT PASSES.`

segments.voice: Pick one small sensation, the breath at the nostrils, warmth in the hands, a pressure where you sit, and watch it arise, shift, fade and arise again; nothing in it holds still. Then, for a breath or two, remember that every person around you right now has a body doing the same. Inside, outside, arising, passing: just enough to know.
Anicca. The sutta's chorus, watched inside yourself and in others: everything arising, everything passing away.
Your line: it arises, it passes. Inside you, and in everyone else. Two hundred fifty, done.

guess: impermanence: everything arises and passes away
a sad belief that nothing in life matters
the idea that the soul lives on forever

251.title: The body: postures
251.hook: walking, he knows he walks; standing, sitting, lying down (MN 10)
251.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay meditators often alternate sitting with walking meditation, pacing a short path slowly and knowing each step, and teachers encourage knowing the posture throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was anicca, the sutta's chorus: inside and outside, arising and passing away. Your line was it arises, it passes. Day two hundred fifty-one.

Quick question, and don't move: how are you sitting right now? Legs crossed? One foot tucked under? Leaning on an elbow? A lot of people have to look down to find out. The whole day is spent in some position, standing in line, slumped on the couch, lying in bed scrolling, and hardly anyone is there for it. The body is in one place, and the mind is somewhere else entirely. The next exercise in the Satipatthana Sutta sounds almost too simple to count.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU SITTING RIGHT NOW?` → `DID YOU HAVE TO LOOK?` → `ALMOST TOO SIMPLE.`

segments.voice: After the breath, the sutta turns to the four postures, in Pali the iriyapatha, the ways of moving. Walking, the practitioner knows, I am walking. Standing, I am standing. Sitting, I am sitting. Lying down, I am lying down. However the body is placed, they know it that way. That's the whole instruction. Then the chorus comes back: inside, outside, arising, passing, not clinging. It's tempting to laugh. Of course I know I'm sitting. But knowing it as a fact and knowing it as an experience are different. One is a thought about the body. The other is being in it: the weight on the seat, the feet on the floor, the slight lean. And the four postures cover your entire life. You are always in one of them. The breath gave you a doorway you can use anytime. The postures give you a second one, bigger and even harder to miss. No cushion or quiet room needed. The checkout line is standing. The drive home is sitting. Falling asleep is lying down. One more gift. Walking meditation, used in many monasteries, draws on lines like this one: monks and nuns walk slowly up and down a path, knowing each step. For some people, walking is easier than sitting still, and the sutta names walking right alongside sitting.
screen: `WALKING, STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN.` · `A FACT, OR AN EXPERIENCE?` · `ALWAYS IN ONE OF FOUR.` · `WALKING COUNTS TOO.` · then, large: `I KNOW I'M SITTING.`

segments.voice: Stay exactly how you are, without fixing your posture first, and just know it: I am sitting, or standing, or lying down. Feel where the body touches the seat, the floor or the bed, and the shape you're making. Then straighten a little, slowly, knowing that too, and settle back into the plain knowing of the posture.
The body, postures. Walking, standing, sitting, lying down: in whatever way the body is placed, know it that way.
Your line: I know I'm sitting. Wherever you are, the posture is already there to know. See you tomorrow.

keeping a straight back so you can meditate well
a set of yoga poses that stretch and strengthen

252.title: The body: clear knowing
252.hook: going and returning, looking, bending, dressing, eating, even in the toilet (MN 10)
252.howItsDone: In many monasteries, clear knowing is practiced through daily chores, eating in silence, and slow, deliberate movement; lay practitioners often choose one routine act, like washing dishes, as a daily reminder.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, postures. Walking, standing, sitting, lying down, each one known. Your line was I know I'm sitting. Day two hundred fifty-two, the end of the first week in the sutta.

Getting dressed. Chewing your food. Going to the toilet. Not what anyone expects to hear about in a teaching on awakening. The Satipatthana Sutta lists them anyway, right in its instructions, next to walking, sitting and falling asleep. It isn't being crude. It's making a point: there's no special room for this practice, no special hour, and no part of the day that doesn't count.
screen: `DRESSING, CHEWING, THE TOILET.` → `RIGHT IN THE INSTRUCTIONS.` → `NO PART OF THE DAY LEFT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the list, in plain words. The practitioner acts with clear knowing when going forward and coming back. When looking ahead and looking away. When bending and stretching a limb. When wearing the robe and carrying the bowl. When eating, drinking, chewing and tasting. When relieving themselves. When walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and staying silent. The word is sampajanna: clear knowing, or full awareness. Knowing what you're doing, and why, while you do it. It's the second word of the refrain you met five days ago, now with a whole section of its own. The commentaries later unpacked it into four kinds: knowing the purpose of an action, knowing whether it's suitable, keeping it within the range of practice, and seeing it without the idea of a solid self behind it. You don't need all four. The simple version is enough: you're there for it. Look back over this week and you'll see the path widening. Satipatthana: one way, four doors. Ardent and gentle. The breath, known long and short, with skill. The chorus: inside and outside, arising and passing. The postures, the whole shape of the body. And now clear knowing, the smallest actions of an ordinary day. The breath was one thread. The postures were four. This is everything else.
screen: `GOING, LOOKING, BENDING, DRESSING, EATING.` · `EVEN IN THE TOILET.` · `SAMPAJANNA: KNOWING WHAT AND WHY.` · `THE WEEK: FROM BREATH TO EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `EVEN THIS.`

segments.voice: Slowly raise one hand and know it rising, turn the palm over and know it turning, lower it and know it lowering. Turn your head a little to one side and back, bend a finger and stretch it, each small movement known while it happens. Then rest your hands and just sit, knowing you're sitting.
Sampajanna. Clear knowing: being there for the smallest actions of the day, from getting dressed to eating to the toilet.
Your line: even this. A dish, a toothbrush, a shoelace: all of it counts. That's day two hundred fifty-two.

guess: knowing what you do, and why, while you do it
a deep trance that shuts out everyday life
a calm mind gained only by sitting still

original.note: Pali sampajañña: clear knowing, full awareness of what you're doing and why.

trapdoor: what you thought: clear knowing is a special meditative state.
what it means: being there for ordinary actions, knowing what you do and why.
what a scholar hears: sampajañña is from sam + pa + jānāti, 'to know thoroughly'; the commentary's four kinds (purpose, suitability, domain, non-delusion) come from Buddhaghosa, not the sutta itself.

sources.ref: Papañcasūdanī (commentary on MN 10), four kinds of clear knowing
sources.work: Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses (Buddhaghosa)
